newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr caught between opposing forces.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr caught between opposing forces.

text.p: The Australian dollar tracked sideways to the midsession but the routine performance belied a backstage struggle as offshore sellers vied to break support.

"There's lots of two-way stuff," said one dealer, reporting demand from local banks and exporters and options-related bids out of Asia. The sellers were led by a who's who of U.S. investment banks, backed-up by Swiss and other Europeans, which seemed to give the bears the weight advantage.
"The selling is in size and looks to be genuine portfolio adjustments, which means it'll probably wear support down in the end," he said, adding the break would likely come overseas.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local dollar was pinned at US$0.7640/45 having hovered in a US$0.7634/50 range all morning after finishing Tuesday at US$0.7650/55 here.

There was further support at US$0.7620 and 76 but bears had their sights on the 1997 low of US$0.7550 reached in February. A breach would take it to levels not seen since February 1996 and risk a return to the 73 cent trough from January that year.

On the topside, it had taken just a couple of days to establish US$0.7675 as important resistance and a break could well force a short squeeze to the US$0.7710/20 area which had been the floor for the dollar ahead of Friday's rate cut.

On the crosses the local currency crept ahead to 89.34/44 yen from 88.70/80 late here Tuesday, matching a rise in US$/yen. Dealers said there was an undercurrent of concern about impending maturities of dual currency samurai bonds, made worse by mistaken press reports of the amount involved.

One Japanese newspaper said bonds worth as much as 90 billion Australian dollars were coming due -- a wild figure which would have come close to half of the country's entire national debt. This was later corrected to 90 billion yen, or a much more manageable A$810 million, but the brief scare served as a taste of things to come later this year.

From October onwards a flood of yen/A$ samurais do mature and if Japanese investors chose not to roll these over or re-invest the money into other A$ assets, the currency could come under pressure against the yen, said dealers.

That could well be the result given last week's Reserve Bank easing had taken Australian official rates to U.S. levels for the first time since the early 1980's. And market rates out to two-years were already below those in the U.S. as the Federal Reserve was widely expected to tighten at least once by October.
In such a case the U.S. dollar would on the surface offer a more attractive home to Japanese funds than the local currency.
The A$ did have a couple of things in its favour, an upbeat outlook for world commodity prices being one.

With the U.S. economy running hot and Japan finally on the road to a sustainable recovery, analysts expected both the demand for and price of commodities to pick up later this year and next. This was important for the dollar since commodities make up more than 60 percent of Australia's exports.
If nothing else, Japanese investors might still see the A$ as a means of diversifying risk given the vast majority of their funds were already in U.S. dollars.
